Mr. T.H. Khan with Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Kazi, Advocates ----- for the Petitioner. 
Mr. Khaondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. Probir Halder, Advocates ----- for the respondent No. 7-18. 
Mr. Zaman Akhtar, A.A.G. ----- for the other respondents.
parties:
Nurul Islam
Vs.
Election Commission Bangladesh and others
full_judgment:
3. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Senior Counsel after taking us through the writ petition referred to some annexure and has submitted that election to the newly created Teknaf Pourashava was held without preparing electoral roll in accordance with the law and the Rules which are in force. In this connection, he has also referred to the decision of this Court given in writ petition No. 860/01 and has submitted that there were some irregularities regarding delimitation of wards of the newly created Teknaf Pourashava and preparation of voter list and the earlier writ petition was filed challenging such irregularities. Next, he has submitted that the Rule in earlier writ petition was discharged on the ground of being infructuous. According to him, the authority misinterpreted this fact of discharge and held the election without correcting the voter list and other irregularities. In this connection, he has pointed out that in that writ petition the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted before the Court that the Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar took necessary steps for holding a meeting in connection with hearing of objections about the voter list of the newly created Teknaf Pourashava. It was also submitted that the Government was taking steps for publishing revised voter list after taking into consideration all relevant objections in respect of the voter list. The Rule was discharged as being infructuous on the ground that Government had taken steps for correction of the voter list. So, according to Mr. T.H. Khan holding of election without correcting the voter list is not in conformity with the observations made by this Court in the previous writ petition. 

 4. Next, Mr. T.H. Khan has submitted that after the discharge of the above writ petition actually the Election Commission and the local authority took steps for hearing of the objections regarding the mistakes in the voter list in this connection, he first referred to Annexure J, J(1), J(2) and also Annexure-O of the supplementary affidavit on behalf of the petitioner. By referring to Annexure J(2) and Annexure-O, the learned Senior Counsel has also submitted that two most competent and responsible local officers such as the Deputy Commissioner and District Election officer in their reports clearly pointed out that there were irregularities in preparation of electoral roll and there were several mistakes. Mr. T.H. Khan has pointed that the report of the Deputy Commissioner was dated 12.3.2002 and report of the District Election officer was dated 21.3.2002 but even after those reports no necessary steps were taken for correction of the voter list, instead, election was held only after few days on 2.4.02. This holding of election, according to Mr. T.H. Khan, is both in violation of provisions of the Pourashava Ordinance and Rules and also in violation of the order of this Court passed in the earlier writ petition. He has also termed this election as malafide. 

 10. It is interesting to note that both the learned Senior Counsels also appeared in Shah Alam's case and made submissions in that case. It appears to us that actually the facts and circumstances of that case are totally different from the facts and circumstances of the present case. Here, we have found that previously a writ petition (W.P. No. 860/02) was filed challenging the delimitation of wards and preparation of the voter list of newly created Teknaf Pourashava. It is clear that this challenge was made before declaration of the election schedule and fixing of the date of election. From the judgment of that case (Annexure G), we find that the Government gave an understanding and even took some steps for correction and revision of the voter list after hearing all objections about the voter list of Teknaf Pourashava. In view of such steps taken by the Government and in view of the understanding given by the Government that voter list would be revised after hearing objections, the learned Advocate for the petitioner prayed for discharging the Rule and accordingly the Rule was discharged as being infructuous. 

 11. So, we find that the matter relating to irregularities in preparation of electoral roll came up for decision before this Court in that writ petition before declaration of the election schedule. In view of the observations, and in view of the submissions, made in that case, it was the legal duty of the respondents including the Election Commission to hold the election after necessary corrections in the voter list on hearing all objections. We have specifically made query to the learned Advocates of the respondents including the learned A.A.G. as to whether such corrections were made in pursuance to the observations of the Court but they could not show anything. However, Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed conceded that corrections were not made. But, he has argued that even if no corrections were made, as the election has already been held, it can not be challenged under writ jurisdiction. 

 12. Mr. Halder has also submitted that though corrections were not made about the mistakes in the voter list, election can not be challenged and in this connection he relied on the case of Nawal Kishore Agarwala Vs. Municipal Board, Gorakhpur and others as reported in AIR 1937 Allahabad 365 and also the case of Pandharinath Gyanoba Rao and others Vs. Manikrao Shamrao and others AIR 1969 Mysore 84. We have perused both the cases. In the case of Allahabad, the election was challenged before a civil court on the ground of mistake or omission in the preparation of the electoral roll. The Court in that case has observed that if there be such mistakes, they would be merely in the nature of irregularity and not an illegality so as to vitiate the election itself. The Court has further observed that such mistakes or irregularities can be taken into account by the Election Tribunal. In the Mysore case, the Court held the view that as there was provision of appeal against the preparation of electoral roll so it was not open to challenge the legality or correctness of electoral roll under Article 329(b) of the Constitution of India. 

 13. We are of the view that the facts and circumstances of both the cited cases are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case before us. We have noticed earlier that the matter came up before this Court long before election process started. In view of the observations made by this Court in the earlier writ petition, the Election Commission and the local authority also took necessary steps for correction of the voter list but instead of actually correcting the voter list, suddenly and abruptly election was held. This amounts to violation of the provisions of law and also disregard to the observations of this Court made in the earlier writ petition. This Court, in the earlier writ petition, did not give any finding on merit but discharged the Rule as being infructuous on the ground that the Government took steps for holding election after disposal of all objections regarding the irregularities about preparation of voter list. Election Commission also took steps for removal of the irregularities. In that judgment there is reference of a notice given by the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar fixing a date of hearing of objections. This notice is dated 1.4.01 (Annexure F). It appears that after discharge of the Rule, the Election Commission under a wrong impression fixed a date for election on 27.2.02 on the ground that the writ petition was discharged and no stay order was in existence. However, from annexure I(1) which is a modified notification of the Returning officer, we find that in this notification there is reference of the fact that the matter relating to irregularities in the preparation of electoral roll was brought to the notice of the Election Commission and as such the Election Commission issued a direction to correct the electoral roll after removing the irregularities and mistakes within 10.3.2002 and thereafter to hold the election. So, from this Annexure I(1) we find that there was a clear direction from the Election Commission that election should be held after correction of the voter list within 10.3.02. Unfortunately, we find nothing in the record and the respondents also could not show whether electoral roll was corrected in compliance with the direction of the Election Commission within 10.3.02. So, we find that election was held both in disregard of the order of this Court and also in violation of the order of the Election Commission. 

 14. It is a interesting to note that the Returning officer in Annexure I (1) with reference to a direction of the Election Commission dated 20.2.02, fixed the fresh date for holding the election on 2.4.2002. It is further interesting to note that this new or fresh date of election was fixed by this notification on the same date i.e., 20.2.2002. When the Election Commission has directed that the election be held after correction of the voter list within 10.3.02, we do not understand how before 10.3.02, the Returning officer could fixed a date fore the election. Returning officer ought to have been satisfied before fixing the date that voter list was corrected within 10.3.02 in compliance with the direction of the Election Commission. It is clear that, the election date was fixed 20 days before expiry of that date. This was done clearly in violation of the direction of the Election Commission. 

 15. From our above discussion, we find that in the instant case before us, election was held in disregard of the order of this Court and also in violation of the order of the Election Commission itself. The Returning officer had no authority to fix a date for election before correction of the voter list. In view of these facts and circumstances, the principle laid down in Shah Alam's case or the principle laid down in the two cases of Indian jurisdiction have no manner of application. We have also noticed that within 10.3.02 irregularities or mistakes in the voter list were not corrected. This is evident from Annexure J(2) and O. In Annexure J(2) the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar after holding an inquiry stated in his report clearly that there were irregularities and mistakes and this report is dated 12.3.02. Annexure 0 is the report of the District Election officer. He also held an inquiry and after holding inquiry he also found many irregularities and mistakes in the voter list and in his report at paragraph 5 he sought necessary instructions of the Election Commission regarding the matter. This report is dated 21.3.02. So, the question of correction of voter list was not decided till 21.3.2002 though there was a direction of the Election Commission to correct the voter list within 10.3.02. Thus we do not understand how and on what basis the Returning Officer fixed the date of election on 2.4.02. This fixing of the date of election is totally arbitrary and in violation of the order issued by the Election Commission. There is nothing before us to show and the respondents also could not show that Election Commission issued any further instruction which was sought by the District Election Officer in his report at paragraph 5. Before receiving further instruction from the Election Commission, it is clear to us that holding of election on 2.4.02 was totally illegal and as such we are of the view that the Rule is liable to be made absolute.
